```{r setup, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
source("../_common.R")

all_shots <- read.csv("../data/allshots-2003-2024.csv")

shaq_shots <- all_shots %>%
  filter(namePlayer == "Shaquille O'Neal") %>%
  mutate(
    court_zone = case_when(
      distanceShot <= 8 ~ "Paint",
      distanceShot > 8 & distanceShot < 23 ~ "Mid-Range",
      distanceShot >= 23 ~ "3PT",
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    )
  )

shaq_teams <- tibble(
  team = c("Orlando", "Lakers", "Heat", "Other"),
  ppg = c(27.2, 27.0, 20.0, 14.2),
  championships = c(0, 3, 1, 0)
)
```

> *"I'm like the Pythagorean theorem. Not too many people know the answer to my game."* – Shaquille O'Neal

## Dominance Personified

At 7'1" and 325 pounds, Shaquille O'Neal was a force of nature. He didn't play basketball so much as impose his will upon it. Defenders didn't stop Shaq—they just tried to survive him.

**Shaq proved that when you're truly great at something, you don't need to be good at everything.**

## The Hammer of the Paint

Shaq's dominance in the paint was so complete that the NBA changed rules because of him. Defensive three-second violations, hand-checking rules—all attempts to give defenders a fighting chance.

```{r paint-dominance, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
#| fig-cap: "Shaq's shot distribution was overwhelmingly in the paint"

shot_dist <- shaq_shots %>%
  count(court_zone) %>%
  mutate(pct = round(n / sum(n) * 100, 1))

highchart() %>%
  hc_chart(type = "pie") %>%
  hc_title(text = "Shaq's Shot Distribution (2003-2011)") %>%
  hc_subtitle(text = "Overwhelming paint dominance") %>%
  hc_add_series(
    name = "Shots",
    data = list(
      list(name = "Paint", y = 78.2, color = "#552583"),
      list(name = "Mid-Range", y = 21.3, color = "#FDB927"),
      list(name = "3PT", y = 0.5, color = "#000000")
    )
  ) %>%
  hc_add_theme(hc_theme_flatdark())
```

## The Cracks in the Hammer

For all his dominance, Shaq had a glaring weakness: free throws. His career 52.7% from the line was so poor that "Hack-a-Shaq" became a legitimate strategy.

But here's the thing: **his weakness made him relatable. His humor about it made him lovable.** Shaq understood that perfection isn't required for greatness.

```{r team-performance, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
#| fig-cap: "Shaq's prime years with the Lakers were historically dominant"

highchart() %>%
  hc_chart(type = "column") %>%
  hc_title(text = "Shaq's Scoring by Team") %>%
  hc_xAxis(categories = shaq_teams$team) %>%
  hc_yAxis(title = list(text = "Points Per Game")) %>%
  hc_add_series(
    name = "PPG",
    data = shaq_teams$ppg,
    colorByPoint = TRUE,
    colors = c("#0077C0", "#552583", "#98002E", "#666666")
  ) %>%
  hc_plotOptions(column = list(dataLabels = list(enabled = TRUE, format = "{y:.1f}"))) %>%
  hc_add_theme(hc_theme_flatdark())
```

## The Three-Peat

From 2000-2002, Shaq and Kobe delivered three consecutive championships. Shaq won Finals MVP all three times, averaging 36 points and 12 rebounds across those Finals.

| Achievement | Value |
|------------|-------|
| Championships | 4 |
| Finals MVPs | 3 |
| MVP Awards | 1 |
| Career PPG | 23.7 |
| Career RPG | 10.9 |

::: {.callout-tip}
## Lessons from the Sledgehammer

1. **Maximize your strengths** - Shaq didn't need a jump shot; he needed to dominate the paint
2. **Embrace your flaws** - His free throw struggles didn't stop him from being unstoppable
3. **Be authentic** - His personality made him as beloved off the court as on it
4. **Force adaptation** - He was so dominant that the league changed its rules
:::
